newsitem.title: USA: No rate change seen at key U.S. Fed meeting.
newsitem.headline: No rate change seen at key U.S. Fed meeting.

text.p: If Federal Reserve policy-makers needed another reason to hold interest rates steady on Tuesday, they got it on Friday when the Dow Jones industrial average suffered its second biggest drop ever.
While the stock market recovered some of its poise on Monday, a rate rise now would trigger an avalanche of selling by increasing the cost of credit, analysts said on Monday.

"A move on Tuesday would send the markets into a tailspin since the only conclusion would be that the economy is growing much faster than anyone believes and there is a real threat that inflation would reaccelerate," said Joel Naroff, an economist for First Union Corp. of Charlotte, N.C.
"I do not believe that the Fed is ready to send that message," he added.
Recent economic data suggest growth is moderate and inflation is steady as the U.S. economy continues its unbridled expansion in its seventh year.

A weakening dollar and mounting concern about the outlook for corporate profits sent U.S. stocks diving on Friday. The Dow Jones industrial average shed more than 247 points to close at 7,694.66, its second biggest point drop in history.

Wall Street was still jittery on Monday, but stocks managed to close in positive territory after a roller coaster day that saw the key blue chip index trade in a 185-point range. It closed up almost 109 points at 7,803.36.
Analysts said higher rates were bound to frighten already nervous investors even further and risk a real crash on Wall Street -- rather than what many described as Friday's Short-term correction.

"Since I thought there was about a zero chance of a Fed move before (Friday), I think there is a less-than-zero chance that they are going to move now," said Bruce Steinberg, chief economist at Merrill Lynch in New York. "They're on hold."

The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee will convene for its one-day meeting on U.S. interest rates, the sixth such session this year, at 9 a.m. 1300 GMT and is expected to announce its decision at 2:15 p.m. 1815 GMT.
A group of 31 economists polled by Reuters unanimously said they expected the Fed to keep the key federal funds rate -- what banks charge each other for overnight loans -- steady at 5.50 percent.

The Fed last changed interest rates on March 25, when it raised the federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point to cool off the economy. The central bank stood pat at the last two rate meetings in May and July, convinced that buyoant growth would return to a more sustainable path by itself.

Gross domestic product, the value of all goods and services produced in the United States, grew an unusually strong 4.9 percent in the first quarter of this year, but growth slowed down to 2.2 percent in the April-July quarter as consumer spending slowed and inventories began building up.
Most analysts expect a rebound in the third quarter, but they are divided over whether it will be strong enough to entice the Fed into raising rates before next year.

"There'll be a pickup from what was a pretty depressed second quarter, but I don't think we're going to see excessive growth in the second half," said Merrill Lynch's Steinberg. "I don't think the Fed is moving this year."
But more than two-thirds of economists polled by Reuters projected the Fed would tighten credit at least once before the end of the year.
The continuing strike at United Parcel Service was expected to take a prominent spot on the FOMC's agenda.

The labor action, now in its 15th day, has hurt businesses across the country and is likely to put another damper on overall business activity. However, a settlement considered favorable to the labor union's demand for higher pay and more full-time jobs could put upward pressure on U.S. labor costs.
The Fed asked UPS last week in a letter to describe the economic impact of the strike. Fed economists are expected to be briefed in detail by company officials before the meeting.
